beats.marks: Say nothing here. This is up while you are being introduced and getting settled. Do not talk over your own title card.

visual.title:
None of this
is accounting.

a.lines:
B.S. Biomedical Engineering
B.A. Business Economics

b.lines:
7× Salesforce Certified · AWS CCP
CompTIA A+, Network+, Security+
ISC2 — CISSP exam passed

visual.tail: Let me tell you why it's all the same job.

beats.opener: Before I get into anything, I want to name the obvious thing about my resume.
beats.rest:
I have a degree in biomedical engineering. I have seven Salesforce certifications and I passed the CISSP exam.

None of that is accounting.
beats.marks: PAUSE — two beats. Hands still. Let the objection land before you answer it.

beats.opener: But I also double majored. Business economics, same four years.
beats.rest:
And that major had accounting classes in it, which at nineteen I did not think much about at all.

So the honest version is: I picked both halves of this job when I was nineteen. Engineering, which is how you build the system. And economics, which is what's moving through it. Then I spent about a decade finding out why.

Let me walk you through that decade.

visual.title:
I was the guy
entering the data.
visual.sub: Lab tech. Bench work. Somebody else's software.

beats.opener: My first job out of school was as a lab tech.
beats.rest:
And I'll be honest about that job, because it matters later — it was not the interesting part. I did bench work. Collected samples, ran assays, and typed numbers into somebody else's software.

I was the guy entering the data.

Hold onto that. Almost everything I've done since comes back to it.
beats.marks: Plant. Say "I was the guy entering the data" plainly — no emphasis. It pays off on the CDTFA slide.

visual.title: Then I touched Excel.
visual.sub: Years of historical preclinical data — toxicology and pharmacology.
visual.tail: Data that had a shape — and a shape that was enforced.

beats.opener: Then I got to Amgen, and the actual work turned out to be Excel.
beats.rest:
They had years of historical preclinical data — drug toxicology and pharmacology studies — sitting in spreadsheets. And a spreadsheet will let you type anything into any cell. Nothing enforces that the number in the box is the right kind of number, or that it belongs to the study you think it belongs to.

So I wrote VBA to pull all of it out and move it into a relational database. Where the data had a shape, and the shape was enforced.

beats.opener: That's the first time I understood what I actually liked. It wasn't the science.
beats.rest: It was that the data was in the wrong shape, and somebody had to fix that.
beats.marks: Do NOT say this is what Vast is going through. Let it sit. Cash it in during Topic 2.

visual.title:
Nobody plans to become
a Salesforce admin.
visual.sub: Contract research organization — sample collection and processing. I volunteered once. Six months later I was the department.

beats.opener: Next was a CRO — a contract research organization. We collected and processed samples for other people's studies.
beats.rest:
They ran on Salesforce and they needed somebody to administer it. I raised my hand, mostly out of curiosity.

That's how you become a Salesforce admin, by the way. Nobody applies for it. You volunteer once, and six months later you are the department.
beats.marks: FIRST LAUGH. Say it flat and dry — do not sell it. Then hold. Do not walk on the laugh.

visual.title: I built the system I used to hate using.

items.lead: LIMS — laboratory information management, on Salesforce
items.sub: Sample intake · chain of custody · what has been run on what

items.lead: I'd used the big ones as a tech
items.sub: They're built for the person signing the purchase order — not the person at the bench with a sample in one hand and a barcode gun in the other.

visual.callout: And I could only build it because I'd been the one using it.

beats.opener: The main thing I built there was a LIMS — laboratory information management system.
beats.rest:
Sample intake, chain of custody, where every sample is, what's been run on it.

Here's the part that matters. I had already used LIMS systems — at Amgen, in the lab, as a tech. I knew exactly what they felt like from the entry side. And the big ones are built for the person who signs the purchase order, not for the person standing at the bench with a sample in one hand and a barcode gun in the other.

So I built the simplified version that fit how the work actually happened.

beats.opener: I built the system I used to hate using.
beats.rest: And I could only do that because I had been the one using it.
beats.marks: PAUSE after the first line. This is one of the two lines carrying the whole section.

visual.title:
I keep automating
the job I just did.
visual.tail: Do the job by hand first. Feel where it hurts. Then build the thing that removes it.

beats.opener: If you've been keeping score, there's a pattern here, and I didn't notice it for years.
beats.rest:
I did the bench work, then I built the lab system. I did the data entry, then I built the database.

Every time, the sequence is identical. Do the job by hand first. Feel exactly where it hurts. Then build the thing that takes it away.

I'm going to come back to this at the very end, when I tell you what I'd do in my first ninety days here. Because that plan isn't a theory I came up with for this interview.

It's just the only way I've ever worked.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE, pass 1 of 3. Returns at the end of Topic 1, and again at the close.

visual.title: Same move. Bigger.

items.sub: Project management for a live practice
Custom survey platform, written in Apex
Automated AR/AP payment sync

visual.callout: The last one is the one that changed everything.

beats.opener: Then ForensisGroup — an expert witness referral firm that ran its whole practice on Salesforce. Same move, bigger scale.
beats.rest: I built PMify, project management for live cases. Survey Builder, a custom survey platform in Apex. And an automated AR/AP payment sync between Salesforce and QuickBooks.

beats.opener: That last one changed my life and I had no idea at the time.
beats.rest:
Because to build it, I had to learn what actually happens to a payment. Not the button — the entry. What gets debited, what gets credited, when it's recognized, and what breaks downstream in the books if I get any of it wrong.

I was building accounting plumbing.

And somewhere in there I noticed I cared more about what was moving through the pipe than about the pipe.
beats.marks: Slow down on "than about the pipe." That's the turn of the whole talk.

visual.title:
I wanted a skill
I could use on anybody.
visual.sub: Everyone has a return. Everyone has books. I came for the practical part — I stayed for the puzzle.

beats.opener: So — why accounting. I'll give you the real reason, and it's less romantic than it sounds.
beats.rest:
I wanted a skill I could use on anybody.

Biomedical engineering, I can help you if you're building a device. Salesforce, I can help you if you run Salesforce. Both of those come with conditions attached — you have to already be a certain kind of person before I'm any use to you.

Everybody files a return. Every business has books. So I went for the most practical version of that I could find.

beats.opener: And then I started studying for the CPA exams, and something happened that I didn't plan on.
beats.rest:
I got curious.

Not about the rules — about the shape of them. Why is it written this way. What was somebody trying to prevent when they drafted this. Who got burned before this existed.

I came for the practical part. I stayed because it turned out to be the most interesting rule system I've ever taken apart.
beats.marks: PAUSE two full beats before "I got curious" — longer than comfortable. RATE: say the cert list fast, say "I got curious" slow. The change IS the emphasis.

visual.title: So I went and got it.

items.sub: My third bachelor's degree.

items.lead: Enrolled Agent — admitted to practice before the IRS
items.sub: Business returns through Form 1120. Trial balance to Schedule L, book-to-tax on the M-1.
Completing the experience requirement.

visual.callout: Nobody needs a CISSP to reconcile a bank account. I sat for it anyway.

beats.opener: So I went and got the rulebook.
beats.rest:
Bachelor's in accounting from WGU, 2024. Enrolled Agent — admitted to practice before the IRS. I prepare business returns up through Form 1120, which means I read small-business books for a living. Trial balance to Schedule L, book-to-tax on the M-1. Books to returns is my normal commute.

And all four CPA exams passed. I'm finishing the experience requirement now.

beats.opener: Full disclosure on this slide, though. That accounting degree is my third bachelor's.
beats.rest:
And I passed the CISSP exam — which, same as the CPA, I don't get to put after my name until somebody endorses the experience.

So I'm currently sitting on two exams and two waiting rooms.

Nobody needs a CISSP to reconcile a bank account. I sat for it anyway.
beats.marks: SECOND LAUGH. Deadpan. No smile until after they react. Never say "I love learning" — the slide makes the point for you.

visual.title:
Now I'm the one
asking to see it.
visual.sub: Sales & use tax auditor, State of California — capital purchases · use tax · audit procedure.

beats.opener: Which brings me to now. I'm a sales and use tax auditor for the State of California.
beats.rest: The work is what it sounds like. I go into a business, I pull their records, and I test them. Capital equipment purchases are a standing part of what I test. So is use tax — which is the tax almost nobody self-reports correctly.

beats.opener: Here's the part I didn't expect about this job.
beats.rest:
I spent about a decade building the systems that produce these records. So now I open somebody's QuickBooks, or their ERP, and I can usually tell how an entry got made. Who made it. What screen they were looking at. Whether anyone ever looked at it again.

I know what it looks like from the inside, because I used to build the inside.
beats.marks: PAUSE — do not rush this. The section has walked ten minutes to get here. This is the payoff of slide 2: "none of this is accounting" — turns out all of it was.

visual.title:
I sing.
I play guitar.
visual.sub: Sometimes both at the same time.

beats.opener: Last thing before I get into the topics. Outside of work I sing, and I play guitar. Sometimes both at the same time.
beats.rest:
And there's a reason I didn't skip this slide. Music is the only other thing I do where the constraints are the entire point. There's a key. There's a time signature. Nobody has ever written a better song by deciding those didn't apply to them. The structure isn't in the way of the interesting part — the structure is what makes the interesting part possible.

That's more or less how I feel about accounting rules. Which I recognize is a strange sentence to say out loud.

So let's talk about one.
beats.marks: PAUSE before "So let's talk about one." That's the transition into Topic 1 — no dead air after it.

visual.title: Capitalize, or expense?

items.sub: What the rule actually asked for
My own contribution, specifically
The result, and whether it held
Lessons — said honestly

visual.callout: Two calls. One from the audit chair. One from the other chair.

beats.opener: Topic one. Capitalize, or expense.
beats.rest:
I'm going to walk you through two calls I've made. For each one I'll give you the same four things: what the requirement actually was, what I personally did about it, how it came out, and what I'd do differently.

The first call I made from the audit chair. Somebody else's books, and I was the one asking the questions.

The second one I made from the other chair.

Same question, both times. They did not feel remotely the same.
beats.marks: "The other chair" stays vague. Do not clarify, do not gesture, do not smile knowingly. You're planting something you won't pay off for ten minutes.

sectionTitle: The spray booth in the repairs account

visual.title:
The spray booth in
the repairs account.
visual.sub: A CDTFA field audit — details disguised.

beats.opener: People think a sales tax audit only looks at sales. It doesn't.
beats.rest: Every field audit examines purchases too.

sectionTitle: The spray booth in the repairs account

visual.kick: Situation · Every audit starts with a split
visual.title: Purchases go in two piles.
visual.tail: That split is a capitalization review — I just come at it from the enforcement side.

beats.opener: Step one is splitting purchases into two piles: fixed assets, and expense items.
beats.rest: That split is a capitalization review. Same question you ask at Vast — is this an asset, or an expense? I just come at it from the enforcement side.

sectionTitle: The spray booth in the repairs account

items.sub: Repairs & maintenance: where assets go to hide.
Use tax never self-assessed.
All on one invoice — a spray booth.
Their own records told on them.

beats.opener: Auto body shop. I'm going through repairs and maintenance, line by line.
beats.rest:
R&M is where assets go to hide — not because people cheat, but because of how bookkeeping happens. I'll come back to that.

And there it is: a twenty-thousand-dollar invoice. Out-of-state vendor. No tax charged. A spray booth — equipment, freight, and installation on one invoice. Coded to repairs. And not on the depreciation schedule.

sectionTitle: The spray booth in the repairs account

items.sub: Not fixing a booth. Acquiring one.
Not months.
Same principle as ASC 360 basis — tax and book agree.

beats.opener: Now I have a call to make — and I have to defend it.
beats.rest:
Repair, or capital asset? If it's an asset, two things follow: it belonged on their books as equipment, and use tax was due — never paid.

Three factors. It added capability — they weren't fixing a booth, they were acquiring one. Useful life in years, not months. And my favorite: their own books contradicted themselves — expensed in R&M, missing from the depreciation schedule they kept for everything else. Their own records told on them.

beats.opener: I called it a capital asset and computed the measure.
beats.rest: Purchase price, plus freight, plus installation — the cost of putting the asset in service. Same rule as ASC 360 basis. Tax and book agree on that one.

sectionTitle: The spray booth in the repairs account

visual.title:
It has to cut
both ways.
visual.sub: The genuine repairs — compressor service, filters — I left alone. If the call only goes one direction, it isn’t judgment.

beats.opener: But the same account had real repairs — and I left those alone.
beats.rest: Compressor service. Filters. Genuinely expenses. If the call only ever goes one direction, it's not judgment — it's a shakedown. A defensible position cuts both ways.

sectionTitle: The spray booth in the repairs account

items.sub: Defended at exit conference; asset capitalized, use-tax accrual set up.
The invoice just landed in the wrong pile — for three years.

items.lead: The decision belongs at the point of entry
items.sub: On purpose, under a written policy. Hold that thought for Topic 2.

beats.opener: At the exit conference, I walked the owner and their CPA through it.
beats.rest: Useful life. Added capability. The full measure. The classification held, the assessment stood — and going forward, the booth went on the books and a use-tax accrual process was set up to catch the next big purchase.

beats.opener: Nobody at that shop was cheating.
beats.rest:
The invoice came from a vendor that sounded like a repair vendor, got filed where repair invoices go, and sat there wrong for three years — until I showed up.

The capitalize-or-expense call was made by default, at data entry, by the person with the least context. The fix isn't better bookkeepers. It's making the call at the point of entry — on purpose, under a written policy. Hold that thought for Topic 2.

sectionTitle: Four months of my own time

visual.title:
Four months of
my own time.
visual.sub: PMify + Survey Builder, built on ForensisGroup’s Salesforce. No consultant invoice — the invoice was me.

beats.opener: My second example is the same question from the opposite chair.
beats.rest: First story: I caught someone else's classification. This time, the cost was my own time — and I'll be straight about how the decision actually got made. That's where the lesson is.

sectionTitle: Four months of my own time

visual.title:
A subscription is never an asset.
The setup might be.
visual.tail: Internal payroll counts — “we didn’t pay a vendor” isn’t an answer.

beats.opener: ForensisGroup runs its practice on Salesforce.
beats.rest: I did systems work for them — built two things on top of that subscription. PMify, a project management system. And Survey Builder, a survey platform I wrote in Apex. About four months of development.

beats.opener: A Salesforce subscription is a cloud computing arrangement — ASC 350-40.
beats.rest: The subscription fee is never an asset — it's rent. But implementation costs — configuration, customization, coding, testing — those are capitalizable. And here's what most people miss: internal payroll counts. The standard doesn't require a consultant's invoice.

sectionTitle: Four months of my own time

visual.kick: Result, then Action · What actually happened
visual.title: Honestly.

items.sub: No capitalization discussion at the time. Nobody asked, including me.
No time records · scoping- and training-heavy mix · immaterial at that scale.

items.lead: “The right answer reached the wrong way”
items.sub: A defensible answer without documentation is still an undocumented answer.

beats.opener: There was no consultant invoice — the invoice was me.
beats.rest: Four months of configuring, customizing, testing. So “we didn't pay anyone” isn't an answer. The question was real: should some of that cost sit on the balance sheet?

beats.opener: Here's what actually happened — no dressing it up.
beats.rest: It ran through payroll and got expensed as incurred. No capitalization discussion. Nobody asked the question — including me. The decision was made by default.

sectionTitle: Four months of my own time

visual.title: Three things.

items.sub: Not to force capitalization — to preserve the option.

items.lead: Write the memo even when the answer is “expense”
items.sub: An hour of work turns a default into a position.
Same framework at Vast — the NetSuite and Ramp implementations lived this exact question.

visual.callout: The twist: a capitalized CCA cost isn’t a fixed asset — it’s a prepaid-type asset amortizing into the same opex line as the subscription. Never depreciation.

beats.opener: What I can stand behind is the conclusion — I've since worked it like an auditor would.
beats.rest:
Measurement: no time records separating dev work from everything else — so any capitalized number would be a reconstruction. I'd never accept one from a taxpayer, so I won't accept one from me.

Stage mix: heavy on scoping up front and training at the end — both expensed under the standard anyway.

Materiality: at that firm's size, the capitalizable slice changes nobody's view of the financials.

beats.opener: Expense was the right answer — reached the wrong way.
beats.rest: A defensible answer without documentation is still an undocumented answer. If an auditor walked in, the position holds — but nobody could hand them the memo that proves it. That's the gap.

beats.opener: Three things I'd do differently.
beats.rest:
Track hours while it's happening — not to force capitalization, to preserve the option. Once the quarter closes, the ability to measure is gone.

Write the memo even when the answer is “expense.” One hour turns a default into a position.

And know when scale flips the answer. At Vast — real invoices, dedicated engineers, material dollars — the same framework lands the other way. You've lived this: someone had to make this exact call on the NetSuite and Ramp implementations.

beats.cue: L · The twist — prepaid, not PP&E
beats.opener: One last twist — a trap I'd want to catch at Vast.
beats.rest: A capitalized CCA cost isn't a fixed asset. It's a prepaid-type asset, amortized into the same opex line as the subscription — never depreciation. Coding it to PP&E is wrong even when capitalizing is right.

sectionTitle: Four months of my own time

visual.title:
Two chairs.
Same principle.
visual.sub: Classify on purpose, at the source, with the documentation to prove it.

beats.opener: Two examples. Two chairs.
beats.rest: An auditor finding an asset hidden in a repairs account. A builder whose own four months became the accounting question. Same principle: classify on purpose, at the source, with proof. Which brings me to what I'd do at Vast.

visual.title:
The first
90 days.
visual.sub: Learn the job honestly. Contribute like a builder.

beats.opener: Topic two: my first ninety days.
beats.rest: Straight up: this is a learning plan and a contribution plan at the same time. You know I haven't done international accounting — so I'll tell you exactly how I get useful fast, and what I bring while I do.

visual.title:
I haven’t done
international accounting.
visual.sub: FAR tested consolidation and currency translation. I understand the concepts in theory. I just don’t have the reps.  —  Yet.

beats.opener: Let me say the obvious part out loud: I haven't done international accounting.
beats.rest:
FAR tested consolidation and currency translation — ASC 830, eliminations, the CTA through OCI. I understand the concepts in theory. I just don't have the reps.

Yet.

But you've already heard how I handle that. I bought the CPA review course before I had the degree. I was handed a tax system I'd never seen and filed two hundred and fifty returns on it in one season.

So here's what I've already started.

visual.title: Four problems, and I know their names.

items.sub: JPY and EUR to USD — the CTA runs through OCI, not the income statement.
Intercompany, investment, minority interest — OneWorld or by hand.
Arm’s-length documentation for Section 482 and French/Japanese review.
VAT and Consumption Tax — the discipline I run daily on CA sales & use tax.

beats.opener: The terrain has four problems, and I already know their names.
beats.rest: Currency translation — ASC 830, and the CTA runs through OCI, not income. Consolidation — intercompany and investment eliminations. Transfer pricing — documentation that survives Section 482 and a foreign authority's review. And indirect tax — VAT and Consumption Tax, the same discipline I run daily on California sales and use tax.

items.lead: Follow Japan’s package all the way through
items.sub: Translation, eliminations, into the consolidated statements — once, manually.
What the auditors asked for last time, and what dragged.
Entities, currencies, elimination rules.

beats.opener: Month one: walk one close by hand.
beats.rest: Follow Japan's reporting package all the way through — translation, eliminations, into the consolidated statements — once, manually, so I know where it breaks. Learn the PBC universe: what the auditors asked for last time, and what dragged. And map how OneWorld is configured — entities, currencies, elimination rules.

items.sub: Mine — checked by someone senior.
Where do the hours actually go?

items.lead: Pick one automation with the controller
items.sub: Highest pain, lowest risk.

beats.opener: Month two: real close tasks, under review.
beats.rest: Reconciliations, translation entries — mine, checked by someone senior. While I'm in there, I time the close: where do the hours actually go? Then I pick one automation with the controller — highest pain, lowest risk.

visual.title: Own my slice. Ship the first automation.

items.sub: No training wheels.
With a before-and-after number.
Well enough to survive me.

beats.opener: Month three: own my slice, ship the first automation.
beats.rest: My close tasks fully mine. The automation live, with a before-and-after number. Both documented well enough to survive me.

visual.kick: While I learn — the builder part
visual.title: Three builds I already know how to make.

items.sub: Every PBC item an owned task with a status. I’m the auditor who sends those lists — I’ve watched what makes a response fast or slow.
Automated completeness and tie-out checks on subsidiary packages, before a human reviews.
Remember the spray booth. Cleaner books upstream is a faster close downstream.

beats.opener: Now the part I bring on day one: the builder part.
beats.rest:
Three builds I already know how to make.

An audit request tracker. Every audit I run starts with me sending a document request — so I've watched, from the other side, exactly what makes a company slow. It's almost never the accounting. It's the coordination: requests scattered across five inboxes, nobody sure what's still outstanding. Every PBC item becomes an owned task with a status, so “where are we” takes four seconds instead of a meeting.

A package pre-check — automated completeness and tie-out checks on subsidiary packages, before a human reviews them.

And point-of-entry classification rules in Ramp — remember the spray booth. Cleaner books upstream is a faster close downstream.

visual.title: A rules layer in front of NetSuite.
visual.tail: Remember the spray booth — this catches it on day one.

beats.opener: Here's build three as a picture.
beats.rest: Flag the two rework patterns before they ever sync to NetSuite, and route them to a short review queue. Fewer reclasses at close, and a cleaner audit trail on the way through.

visual.title:
Before the audit
shows up.
visual.sub: As Vast scales, the auditors get bigger and the PBC list gets longer. Someone inside has to already speak that language. I’d go get the Certified Internal Auditor — not because the role asks for it, but because I’d rather be that person before the audit arrives than during it.

beats.opener: One more thing, and this one's past the ninety days.
beats.rest:
As Vast scales, the auditors get bigger and the PBC list gets longer. Somebody inside has to already speak that language — to know what they're going to ask for before they ask.

I'd go get the Certified Internal Auditor for that. Not because the role requires it. Because I'd rather be that person before the audit shows up than during it.

visual.title:
Instrument
the close.
visual.sub: Books-to-reports as a pipeline: measure where the hours go, then remove one manual step every month — each build shipped with a before/after number.

beats.opener: Which is the real idea: instrument the close.
beats.rest:
Treat books-to-reports like a pipeline. Measure where the hours go, then remove one manual step every month — small builds, each shipped with a before-and-after number.

Most closes never get faster because nobody owns “faster.” I'm offering to own it.

visual.sub: My close tasks owned. One automation live, with numbers. And a close that gets a step faster every month after that.

beats.opener: So, in ninety days:
beats.rest: My close tasks owned. One automation live, with numbers. And a close that gets a step faster every month after that.
